The draft law that is expected to put the peace process between the Turkish state and the PKK into practice has been signed by the majority of political parties in the Turkish Parliament. The “Law Proposal on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration” opens an important door as an initial step. But we must remember that this legislation is not a comprehensive macro-level framework that solves the entire process by itself. So it is too soon to criticize the lack of some long-term things at this point, because, as I said, this is not intended to be a complete political settlement document. Rather, it should be seen as a practical point of departure for initiating the process and in that sense it constitutes a constructive and meaningful first step. The proposal is not an amnesty law, technically. It is structured so as to create a process of social reintegration and to create the conditions for greater acceptance and consensus. This is also confirmed by the provisions on the suspension of criminal proceedings and sentences. Subsequently, amendments to the Turkish Penal Code and other relevant legislation may, where applicable, address issues such as the restoration of restricted political rights. In this respect, the proposal might form a basis for a gradual move towards wider democratization measures. Regarding weapons surrender, heavy weaponry, facilities, and existing inventories beyond individual surrender processes would likely be coordinated by Turkey’s intelligence and military institutions. This aspect may have been intentionally excluded from the text as part of operational security (OPSEC) considerations in a post-conflict normalization process. Ultimately, the proposal appears to be a framework that allocates responsibilities and administrative roles to the relevant parties regarding how the process will be managed and implemented. Hopefully, this marks a constructive beginning.
